questiontext.text: Iterative depth-first maze solving uses which structure to remember the current path?

feedback.text: Correct — the current cell/move is pushed onto a stack.
A queue gives breadth-first search, not iterative DFS backtracking.
No priorities are involved in plain DFS backtracking.

answer.text: A hash map keyed by distance

feedback.text: Distance keying is not how the path is tracked here.

generalfeedback.text: Iterative DFS pushes each visited cell/move onto a stack so it can backtrack later.

questiontext.text: What happens at a dead end during stack-based maze solving?

answer.text: Pop the stack to backtrack to the previous cell

feedback.text: Correct — popping returns to the last cell with unexplored options.

answer.text: Push a new random cell onto the stack

feedback.text: Backtracking pops; it does not jump to a random cell.

answer.text: Clear the entire stack and restart

feedback.text: You only unwind one step at a time, not the whole path.
A dead end only ends the current branch, not the whole search.

generalfeedback.text: On a dead end you pop the stack, backtracking to the previous cell to try another direction.

questiontext.text: In stack-based maze solving, what is pushed onto the stack as you advance?

answer.text: The current cell (or move) being explored

feedback.text: Correct — the path of cells/moves is stored on the stack.

answer.text: The total number of dead ends found so far

feedback.text: A running count is not what drives backtracking.

answer.text: The Manhattan distance to the exit

feedback.text: Plain DFS backtracking does not store distances.
That is unrelated to path tracking.

generalfeedback.text: Each current cell or move is pushed so the algorithm can pop and backtrack later.

questiontext.text: Overall, stack-based maze solving is an iterative form of which traversal?

feedback.text: Correct — a stack yields depth-first exploration with backtracking.
BFS uses a queue and explores level by level.
That needs a priority queue and edge weights.
Level-order is a queue-based BFS pattern, not stack-based DFS.

generalfeedback.text: Using a stack to go deep and backtrack is exactly iterative depth-first search.

questiontext.text: Cells are marked as visited to avoid revisiting them and getting stuck in cycles.

feedback.text: Correct — marking visited cells prevents cycles and redundant work.
Without a visited mark the search could loop forever.

questiontext.text: Stack-based maze solving explores all neighbors level by level, exactly like breadth-first search.

feedback.text: Level-by-level is BFS; a stack gives depth-first exploration.
Correct — a stack explores one path as deep as possible, then backtracks.

questiontext.text: Going as deep as possible and returning on a dead end is called ______.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about stack-based maze solving are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: On a dead end it pops the stack to backtrack

feedback.text: Yes — popping unwinds to the previous decision point.

answer.text: It explores one path as deep as possible before trying alternatives

feedback.text: Yes — that is depth-first behavior.

answer.text: It guarantees the shortest path in an unweighted maze

feedback.text: No — that is BFS; DFS finds a path, not necessarily the shortest.

answer.text: It requires a priority queue ordered by distance

feedback.text: No — a plain stack suffices; no priorities are needed.

generalfeedback.text: Stack-based DFS: push moves, pop to backtrack on dead ends, go deep first; it does not guarantee shortest paths.
